specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper evaluates character-level encoder–decoder LSTM models for historical spelling normalization across 43 Early New High German texts, comparing single-task and multi-task (grapheme→phoneme using CELEX) variants and ablating beam search, lexical filtering, attention, and bidirectional encoding. Evidence in Tables 1 and 4 supports that encoder–decoder variants outperform several baselines on average (claim C1). MTL with CELEX yields average gains, particularly for non-attentional models (claim C2); the reported MTL GREEDY/BEAM numbers are higher than corresponding base variants and MTL without attention attains parity with single-task attention in averages. Ablations show cumulative gains from beam/filter/attention in single-task setups (claim C3), documented in the progressive averages. Combining MTL with explicit attention does not produce additive gains and sometimes reduces performance (claim C4): Table 1 and per-text Table 4 show modest average drops when adding attention to MTL. The authors present multiple correlational diagnostics (parameter-difference correlations, error-overlap, high κ agreement, saliency correlations, t-SNE) as converging evidence that MTL induces attention-like focusing strategies (claim C5). These diagnostics are meaningful and consistent with the hypothesis but heterogeneous (wide variance) and do not establish causal mechanistic equivalence. Major methodological caveats affect interpretation: hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript (B) applied corpus-wide (A2), lexical filtering that excludes some targets (A5), fixed MTL sampling strategy (A8), CELEX modern pronunciations possibly mismatching historical orthography/dialects (A3), and selection of diagnostic subsets (saliency computed only when models agree). I mark which claims are supported, partially supported, or overstated in the identified-claims section below and provide concrete, evidence-based suggestions and alternative interpretations.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Problem: Historical spelling normalization has scarce per-text data => need architectures that work on small datasets.
L2: Approach: Use character-level encoder–decoder LSTMs, augment with beam search, lexical filter, attention, bidirectional encoder to improve single-task performance.
L3: Auxiliary signal: Use grapheme-to-phoneme CELEX data in MTL to inject phonological inductive bias that may regularize learning and focus decoding.
L4: Empirical test: Train/evaluate on 43 Anselm texts with held-out 1,000-token tests; compare baselines and model variants (Tables 1,4).
L5: Observation: Encoder–decoder variants outperform baselines on average => claim C1 supported by aggregate results (Table 1,4).
L6: Observation: MTL improves non-attentional models and matches attention-enabled single-task model on averages => claim C2 supported in aggregate but heterogeneous per-text.
L7: Observation: Beam, lexical filter, attention, bidirectional encoding give cumulative gains in single-task chain => claim C3 supported by progression in Table 4.
L8: Observation: Adding attention to MTL does not add gains and sometimes hurts => claim C4 partially supported; effect small/variable and hyperparam sensitivity not explored.

L9: Diagnostic analyses (parameter correlations, error overlap, saliency, t-SNE) show similarities between MTL and attention behaviors => claim C5 partially supported by correlational evidence but causality not established.
L10: Conclusion: MTL provides beneficial inductive bias for low-data normalization and may implement focusing mechanisms similar to attention; further causal probing recommended.

identified_claims.claim_text: Character-level encoder–decoder models outperform established baselines (Norma, averaged perceptron, deep bi-LSTM tagger) on historical spelling normalization across 43 Anselm texts (average word-level accuracy improvements shown in Tables 1 and 4).
evidence: Table 1: Base BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION = 82.72% vs Norma 77.89%; averaged perceptron 75.72%; bi-LSTM tagger 79.91%.
Table 4: Per-text results show many texts where encoder–decoder variants exceed baselines.
uncertainty_flags: Averages exclude manuscript B (used for hyperparameter tuning); effect of exclusion not fully quantified.
No paired statistical tests across manuscripts reported to establish significance of average differences.
Per-text heterogeneity: some texts show smaller gains or different performance orderings.

identified_claims.claim_text: Multi-task learning with CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary data improves normalization performance, particularly for models without explicit attention; MTL without attention attains comparable average performance to single-task models with attention.
evidence: Table 1: Base GREEDY 78.91% -> MTL GREEDY 80.64%; Base BEAM+FILTER 80.46% -> MTL BEAM+FILTER 82.76%.
Text statement: 'multi-task architecture without attention performs on-par with the single-task architecture with attention.'
uncertainty_flags: Improvements vary across texts (Table 4 shows heterogeneity; some texts have comparable or no improvements).
MTL training sampling (1 auxiliary per main sample) fixed; sensitivity to different sampling ratios not explored.
Benefit might derive from additional data/regularization generally, not specifically from phonological signal of CELEX — no alternative auxiliary tasks tested.

identified_claims.claim_text: In single-task encoder–decoder models, beam search, lexical filtering, attention (with bidirectional encoder) yield cumulative gains in word-level accuracy.
evidence: Table 4 progression: Base GREEDY 78.91% -> BEAM 79.27% -> BEAM+FILTER 80.46% -> BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION 82.72% (average).
Sample predictions illustrate fewer nonsensical outputs after filtering/beam/attention.
uncertainty_flags: Bidirectional encoder is introduced only in the attentional variant; effect of bidirectionality isolated from attention is not fully reported.
Interactions among components not exhaustively explored (e.g., different filter lexicons, beam sizes, attention hyperparameters).

identified_claims.claim_text: Combining MTL and explicit attention does not yield additive gains; adding attention to the MTL model can reduce performance compared to MTL without attention.
evidence: Table 1: MTL BEAM+FILTER = 82.76% vs MTL BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION = 82.02% (average).
Per-text Table 4 shows cases where MTL+ATT scores slightly lower than MTL without ATT.
uncertainty_flags: Average reduction is modest and variable across texts; some texts show parity or slight improvement with MTL+ATT.
No hyperparameter sweep for attention under MTL reported — MTL may interact with attention hyperparameters differently.
Possible confound: when attention is added authors also add bidirectional encoder — architectural changes coupled with MTL complicate attribution.

identified_claims.claim_text: MTL appears to induce internal focusing strategies similar to learned attention: reported correlated parameter changes, overlap in corrected/introduced errors, high output agreement (κ≈0.834), and saliency-map correlations support resemblance.
evidence: Parameter differences: mean Pearson r = 0.346 (std 0.315) across datasets comparing changes vs base; example N4 heatmap correlation ρ = 0.959.
Error analysis: attention resolves 47.7 errors on average, MTL 45.4; overlap in resolved errors 27.7; introduced errors overlap 11.8; κ=0.834 agreement.
Saliency: example correlation ρ = 0.615; systematic analysis across ~19k word pairs (models agreeing) gives mean ρ = 0.303 (±0.177) for attentional vs MTL when input length ≥ 7.
uncertainty_flags: Correlational evidence is heterogeneous (wide std dev, varying per dataset); some high correlations appear anecdotal.
Saliency analysis restricted to examples where models agree; may bias toward similarity and omit informative discordant cases.
Correlation ≠ causation: observed alignment could result from shared inductive biases or output constraints rather than MTL implementing the same computational mechanism as attention.
t-SNE and first-derivative saliency are exploratory, sensitive to choices (perplexity, seeds) and known to be noisy/interpretationally limited.

identified_claims.claim_text: MTL using CELEX pronunciation auxiliary data helps mitigate scarcity of annotated normalization data and yields practical gains on small per-text datasets (4.2k–13.2k tokens), improving average word accuracy.
evidence: Dataset sizes described in Sec. 2; CELEX auxiliary set of 365,530 wordforms.
Table 1 and 4 show higher average accuracies for MTL variants over base models.
uncertainty_flags: Benefit attribution specifically to CELEX phonological signal vs general data-augmentation/regularization not isolated; no control auxiliary tasks (e.g., character LM) tested.
MTL sampling/hyperparameter sensitivity not explored; gains might depend on training regimen choices.

strengths.title: Extensive per-text empirical benchmark
strengths.description: Evaluation covers 43 small historical texts with per-text train/test splits, providing broad evidence of model behavior across diverse dialects.
evidence: Tables 3 and 4: per-text results across 43 Anselm texts with averages and std. dev.
Manuscript describes dialectal coverage and token counts (Sec. 2).

strengths.title: Systematic architectural ablations
strengths.description: Authors evaluate beam search, lexical filtering, attention, bidirectional encoder, and MTL, enabling insight into component contributions.
evidence: Table 4: progressive evaluation of GREEDY, BEAM, BEAM+FILTER, BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION for base and MTL models.
Sec. 3 describes architectural design choices.

strengths.title: Multi-pronged diagnostic analyses
strengths.description: Use of parameter-difference correlations, error-overlap statistics, saliency maps, and t-SNE offers converging, interpretable evidence for representational/behavioral similarities between MTL and attention.
evidence: Sec. 5 subsections and Figures 4–5 with reported correlations and example visualizations.
Reported κ agreement, error-resolved/introduced counts.

strengths.title: Reproducibility effort
strengths.description: Implementation released and paper provides model/hyperparameter details (embedding sizes, dropout, optimizer), supporting replication.
evidence: Sec. 3.7 Implementation in Keras; Sec. 3.6 hyperparameters provided; claim of public code release in Introduction/Conclusion.

concerns.title: Hyperparameters tuned on single manuscript (development bias)
concerns.description: All hyperparameters were chosen manually on manuscript B and then applied unchanged across the other 43 texts; if B is atypical this could bias results and affect cross-text comparability.
evidence: Sec. 3.6: 'We used a single manuscript (B) for manually evaluating and setting the hyperparameters. This manuscript is left out of the averages reported below.'
Shared analysis notes A2 and prior reviewers flagged tuning-on-one-dev risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Perform cross-validation or at least a small hyperparameter sweep on a subset of diverse texts (e.g., stratified by dialect/size) and report sensitivity of key comparisons (base vs MTL, MTL vs MTL+ATT). Alternatively, report paired significance tests across manuscripts using current hyperparameters.

concerns.title: Correlation-based diagnostics lack causal probing
concerns.description: Parameter correlations, saliency similarities, and output overlaps are consistent with the MTL-induces-attention hypothesis but do not establish mechanistic equivalence or causal direction.
evidence: Sec. 5 reports Pearson/ρ correlations with wide std. dev and selective examples (e.g., N4 ρ=0.959 anecdotal) and saliency restricted to examples where all models agree.
Shared analysis A6 notes correlation ≠ causation risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include causal-style probes: (a) lesion/shared-layer ablations (freeze or remove shared encoder components) to see whether MTL's gains disappear; (b) train attention under MTL with separate attention hyperparameter sweeps; (c) test saliency/attention comparisons on disagreeing outputs and on controlled synthetic inputs where attention patterns are known.

concerns.title: Auxiliary-task specificity not isolated
concerns.description: No experiments compare CELEX G2P auxiliary task against alternative auxiliaries (character LM, autoencoding, morphological tags), so it's unclear whether gains come from phonology specifically or from generic multi-task regularization/additional data.
evidence: Sec. 3.5 describes CELEX MTL but manuscript lacks control auxiliary-task experiments; shared analysis A3 & C6 note this.
Authors do not report ablations using different auxiliary datasets or tasks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add at least one control auxiliary task (e.g., character-level language modeling on CELEX orthographic forms, or autoencoding) to measure whether phonological signal produces greater transfer than generic auxiliary supervision.

concerns.title: Lexical filter excludes targets (output constraint confound)
concerns.description: Lexical filtering uses CELEX+training targets, which makes 2.25% of test targets unreachable; such output constraints can artificially raise word-level accuracy for filtered models and bias comparisons.
evidence: Sec. 3.3 notes 2.25% of test targets unreachable due to lexicon (Latin forms); Table 4 shows gains from adding filter.
Shared analysis A5 flags lexicon coverage risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results without lexical filtering and report coverage loss (targets removed). Also report filtered-model accuracy both conditional on reachable targets and unconditional, to quantify inflation. Consider expanding lexicon or using softer lexicon priors rather than hard pruning.

concerns.title: Saliency/t-SNE analyses selective and potentially unstable
concerns.description: t-SNE visualizations and first-derivative saliency are presented for illustrative examples but are sensitive to hyperparameters and were computed only on agreeing outputs, limiting generality.
evidence: Sec. 4.2 and 5.3 use t-SNE (perplexities noted) and Li et al. saliency on examples and a subset (19k agreeing word pairs); shared analysis A9 points to t-SNE/saliency limitations.
Reported saliency mean correlations have large variance (±0.177).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report robustness checks: multiple random seeds/perplexities for t-SNE, bootstrap confidence intervals for saliency correlations, and saliency comparisons including disagreeing outputs. Consider complementary probing methods (e.g., attention-perturbation tests, input masking) that are less noisy.

concerns.title: Statistical testing across manuscripts missing
concerns.description: The paper reports averages and std. dev. across 43 texts but lacks paired statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon/pairwise t-tests) to establish that observed average gains are significant across manuscripts.
evidence: Tables 1 and 4 show means and std. dev. but no p-values or paired tests; prior reviewers suggested this.
Per-text heterogeneity noted (some texts with small/no gains).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run paired significance tests across manuscripts for key comparisons (Base vs MTL, Base+ATT vs MTL, MTL vs MTL+ATT) and report effect sizes/CI to support aggregate claims.

concerns.title: Compatibility of CELEX pronunciations with historical data not demonstrated
concerns.description: CELEX encodes modern German pronunciations; manuscript does not evaluate dialectal/temporal mismatch risk or how CELEX mappings relate to Early New High German spellings.
evidence: Sec. 2 motivates phonology-orthography relation but does not present analyses of CELEX-historical alignment (assumption A3).
Prior-stage reviewers flagged auxiliary-data compatibility risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide qualitative examples of CELEX pronunciations aligning to historical spellings, or quantify transfer by measuring MTL effect size stratified by apparent dialectal distance/orthographic divergence. If possible, include a small filtered CELEX subset adjusted for historical orthography or dialect variants.

concerns.title: MTL sampling and training regimen sensitivity untested
concerns.description: MTL alternates one auxiliary example per main-task sample and counts epochs by main-task size; no exploration of other sampling ratios or scheduler that could modulate transfer strength.
evidence: Sec. 3.5 and 3.6 describe sampling convention; shared analysis A8 notes potential sensitivity.
No ablation varying auxiliary/main sample ratios reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments varying auxiliary:main sampling ratios, or run weighted loss/oversampling experiments to test sensitivity and find robust regimes; report whether observed MTL benefits are stable.

concerns.title: 1,000-token test split stability and representativeness
concerns.description: Using fixed 1,000-token test sets per text may produce high variance estimates for some smaller texts; risk that held-out set not representative of distribution.
evidence: Sec. 4: per-text splits use 1,000 tokens for test and dev; training sizes vary; shared analysis A1 notes representativeness risk.
Std. dev. across texts suggests heterogeneity in performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results averaged over multiple random train/dev/test splits or provide bootstrap confidence intervals per text to show estimate stability. Alternatively, justify 1,000-token choice with variance analysis.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct baseline for sequence-labeling normalization with bidirectional LSTMs and MTL variants
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar target task (historical normalization) and use of neural sequence models; differs by modeling framing (sequence-labeling vs encoder–decoder) and the specific auxiliary tasks evaluated.

comparable_works.relevance: Established rule/Levenshtein-based baseline for normalization
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Non-neural baseline; manuscript reports consistent superiority of neural encoder–decoder models over Norma.

comparable_works.citation_label: Character-level SMT works (Pettersson et al., Sánchez-Martínez et al.)
comparable_works.relevance: Prior approaches framing normalization as character-based SMT
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Conceptually similar (seq2seq transduction) but uses SMT rather than neural encoder–decoder; the current paper substitutes neural networks for SMT and reports improved/competitive results.

comparable_works.relevance: Method for first-derivative saliency used in analysis
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides the saliency approach used; known limits of saliency interpretation apply.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational MTL theory and inductive bias motivation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides theoretical motivation for MTL as an inductive bias that could emulate attention-like functions; manuscript invokes Caruana to support hypothesis.

uncertainty_flags: Heterogeneity across manuscripts (wide std. dev. and per-text variation) weakens strength of corpus-wide averages.
Hyperparameter tuning on one manuscript (B) may bias results and needs sensitivity analysis.
Correlation-based diagnostics (parameter, saliency, error overlap) cannot establish causal/mechanistic equivalence between MTL and explicit attention.
Lexical filtering removes some target forms (2.25%), potentially inflating filtered-model accuracy.
MTL benefits may arise from generic auxiliary-data regularization rather than phonological signal specifically; control auxiliaries not tested.
alternative_interpretations: MTL improvements arise from general regularization/extra-data effects: adding any large auxiliary dataset (not necessarily phonology) could reduce overfitting and improve accuracy; CELEX choice may be incidental.

High output agreement and parameter correlations reflect convergent solutions under shared loss landscapes and lexicon constraints, not identical internal computations—MTL may bias encoder representations toward features that correlate with attention-weighted encodings without implementing an explicit attention mechanism.
Lexical filtering plus MTL together restrict output hypothesis space; gains could be due partly to output pruning rather than better internal focusing.

MTL+attention degradations could stem from suboptimal attention hyperparameters when training with auxiliary supervision (interaction effects), or from overconstraining the shared representation (competing gradients) rather than MTL literally making attention redundant.
transparency_notes: Implementation in Keras is provided; paper lists many hyperparameters (embedding/recurrent size 128, dropout 0.3, Adam lr 0.003, batch size 50, epochs 50) but random seeds, exact preprocessing scripts, and full evaluation scripts for diagnostics should be included for full reproducibility.

Manuscript reports per-text tables (supplementary) which aid verification; authors should explicitly release the code that computes parameter-difference correlations, saliency maps, and error-overlap statistics to permit replication of diagnostic claims.
Authors note lexical filter makes 2.25% of targets unreachable; they should provide per-text counts and versions of main tables without filter to quantify impact.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The pairing of grapheme-to-phoneme CELEX auxiliary task with encoder–decoder normalization is not widely documented in prior work and thus represents a novel inductive-bias approach; novelty alone does not validate mechanistic claims—empirical and causal controls are required to establish whether the auxiliary task provides phonology-specific transfer or only generic regularization.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If CELEX pronunciations align sufficiently with the phonological drivers of orthographic variation in each historical text, MTL will provide targeted inductive bias that improves normalization.
If MTL sampling ratio and shared-layer capacity are tuned per text or per dialect cluster, gains will be larger and more consistent across heterogeneous manuscripts.

If attention hyperparameters are carefully tuned under MTL, combining the two may provide complementary benefits rather than degradation, showing that previously observed non-additivity was a hyperparameter artifact.
If diagnostic causal probes (lesions, interventions) show that disabling shared MTL components removes focusing behavior, then mechanistic claims will be supported.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Encoder–decoder models and MTL are established; applying CELEX G2P as an auxiliary task for historical normalization across many small texts and documenting the specific interaction with attention is an incremental yet useful empirical innovation.
evidence: Prior works used character-level SMT and sequence-labeling (Pettersson et al., Bollmann & Søgaard), but CELEX MTL pairing for historical normalization is absent in cited literature.
uncertainty_flags: Absence of many close analogs in retrieved corpus may reflect novelty but also indexing gaps; robustness of novelty claim depends on how unique CELEX use is in historical-normalization literature.

novelty_lenses.lens: disruptive_novelty (mechanistic claim about MTL learning attention)
novelty_lenses.rationale: If MTL truly induces attention-like focusing mechanisms that can replace explicit attention, this would be a conceptually significant finding affecting model design; current evidence is suggestive but correlational and heterogeneous, so the disruptive claim is not yet fully substantiated.
evidence: Converging diagnostics (parameter correlations, saliency similarity, error overlap, κ agreement) point toward resemblance between MTL and attention behavior.
uncertainty_flags: Correlational nature of evidence, selection biases (saliency only on agreeing outputs), and lack of causal interventions leave the disruptive claim tentative.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (~mid-range) in the empirical claims that encoder–decoder models outperform baselines (supported by aggregate data) and that MTL provides average improvements for non-attentional models. Confidence is reduced by methodological issues: single-dev hyperparameter tuning, lack of statistical testing across manuscripts, lexicon pruning effects, absence of control auxiliary tasks, and correlational diagnostic limitations. Addressing the actionable suggestions would substantially increase confidence.

consensus_findings: Character-level encoder–decoder seq2seq models achieve higher mean word-level accuracy than the cited baselines (Norma, averaged perceptron, deep bi-LSTM tagger) across the reported 43 Early New High German texts.

Multi-task learning (MTL) using the CELEX grapheme→phoneme auxiliary dataset yields average improvements over single-task base models, with the largest relative gains for models without explicit attention (MTL (no-attn) often reaches parity with single-task + attention in aggregate).

In single-task setups, adding beam search, lexical filtering (CELEX + training targets), and attention (with bidirectional encoder where used) produces cumulative average gains in word-level accuracy.
Combining MTL and explicit attention does not produce consistent additive gains on the reported setup; on average MTL+attention performs similarly or slightly worse than MTL without attention.

The paper presents multiple, converging correlational diagnostics (final-layer parameter-change correlations, error-overlap counts, high output agreement κ, saliency-map correlations, t-SNE visualizations) that are consistent with a resemblance between MTL-induced representations/behavior and that of attention-enabled models.
There is substantial heterogeneity across manuscripts: many reported metrics (accuracies, correlations) show large variance across texts, so aggregate means mask per-text variability.

Methodological choices that materially affect interpretation are clearly documented (hyperparameters set on a single dev manuscript B, lexical filtering that excludes some targets, MTL sampling regimen), but several of these choices create potential confounds that require controlled follow-ups.
disagreements: Strength of mechanistic claim: reviewers agree diagnostics are suggestive but disagree in how strongly the paper should state that 'MTL learns attention' mechanistically. Some characterize the evidence as promising but preliminary and require causal probes; others note the convergent diagnostics give plausible support contingent on additional controls.

Interpretation of the non-additivity of MTL+attention: some reviewers consider the observed small average drop as possibly a hyperparameter/tuning artifact, while others treat it as meaningful evidence of redundancy or interference between MTL and attention. Both interpretations are retained as plausible given current evidence.

Novelty framing: reviewers concur the empirical application (CELEX G2P as auxiliary for historical normalization across many small texts) is novel relative to the immediate literature, but they differ on whether the mechanistic claim—if validated—would be disruptive. The manuscript's novelty is widely viewed as an incremental methodological contribution unless stronger mechanistic proof is provided.
uncertainty_hotspots: Causality vs correlation: parameter correlations, saliency-map similarity, and error overlaps are correlational; they do not by themselves establish that MTL implements the same functional mechanism as explicit attention.

Auxiliary-task specificity: it is unclear whether observed MTL gains are specific to CELEX grapheme→phoneme supervisory signal (phonology-driven inductive bias) or would equally arise from other large auxiliary datasets/tasks (generic data/regularization effect).

Hyperparameter generalization: all hyperparameters were tuned manually on a single manuscript (B) excluded from averages; sensitivity of key comparisons (MTL vs attention, MTL+attention interaction) to alternative hyperparameter choices is unknown.

Lexical-filter confound: hard lexical filtering (lexicon = CELEX + training targets) makes a non-negligible fraction of targets unreachable (authors report ~2.25%); the impact of pruning on reported word-accuracy gains is not fully quantified.
Selection bias in diagnostics: saliency correlations were computed on subsets where models agree on outputs; this selection may bias diagnostics toward easier cases and overstate similarity.

Per-text heterogeneity: high variance across manuscripts means average results may obscure systematic failures or subsets where MTL hurts rather than helps; robustness across dialectal/time splits is uncertain.

Reproducibility of diagnostics: visualization-dependent analyses (t-SNE, first-derivative saliency) can be sensitive to seeds and hyperparameters; exact reproducibility details for these diagnostics are incomplete.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-focused reviewers prioritized coherence of the experimental chain and highlighted missing causal controls (lesions, interventions) needed to move from correlation to mechanism.

Methodology/auditors emphasized reproducibility and validity issues (single-dev hyperparameter tuning, lack of paired statistical tests, sampling regimen sensitivity, and lexicon coverage), driving requests for robustness analyses and explicit statistical testing.

Novelty assessors (incremental and disruptive lenses) emphasized the contribution's placement in the literature: novelty primarily in the empirical pairing of CELEX G2P MTL with encoder–decoder normalization and the diagnostic framing; their emphasis varied between treating the work as a valuable empirical increment versus a potentially disruptive hypothesis needing stronger evidence.

Claim verifiers synthesized the above to underline which claims are empirically supported (performance improvements) versus those that are partially supported or overinterpreted (mechanistic equivalence).

These role-specific emphases produced complementary critiques rather than contradicting facts: methodological reviewers drove requests for controls and statistical rigor, structural reviewers demanded causal probing for mechanistic claims, and novelty reviewers contextualized the contribution's originality.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center the editorial decision on whether the manuscript provides sufficient empirical evidence and controls for its strongest interpretive claim (that MTL induces attention-like focusing). If the paper's principal value is the empirical benchmark and method variant (encoder–decoder + CELEX MTL) rather than a definitive mechanistic discovery, ensure final presentation frames mechanistic claims as tentative and conditional. Recommended items for the authors before major editorial progression: (a) provide paired statistical tests (non-parametric recommended) across the 43 manuscripts for key model comparisons and report effect sizes/CIs; (b) quantify the impact of lexical filtering (report results without filter; enumerate unreachable targets per text and their characteristics); (c) run sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters (tune on multiple dev texts or perform limited cross-validation) and report whether main comparisons (Base vs MTL, MTL vs MTL+ATT) hold; (d) add control auxiliary-task experiments (at least one non-phonological auxiliary, e.g., character LM or autoencoder, and a randomized-label CELEX control) or provide rationale/analysis showing CELEX-specific signal is likely driving gains; (e) include causal-probing experiments that bear on the mechanistic claim (e.g., lesion/freeze shared MTL layers, test attention under re-tuned hyperparameters, compare saliency vs attention on disagreeing outputs); (f) furnish reproducibility materials for diagnostics (random seeds, scripts for saliency and t-SNE, exact preprocessing) and report robustness checks for visualization-based analyses; (g) report stratified performance (e.g., by word length, dialect/period clusters) to clarify heterogeneity. Keep the editor role central: assess whether authors' revisions address the most critical validity threats (statistical robustness, auxiliary-task specificity, causal probes) and whether claims are scaled accordingly in the text.
meta_review.author_guidance: Prioritize revisions that materially reduce interpretive uncertainty and enable readers/editors to judge the mechanistic claim fairly. Actionable steps: 1) Statistical rigor: run paired significance tests across manuscripts for the principal comparisons (Base vs Best ED, Base vs MTL, MTL vs MTL+ATT), report p-values and effect sizes, and provide bootstrapped confidence intervals for mean accuracies. 2) Hyperparameter sensitivity: validate that hyperparameters tuned on manuscript B generalize—either (a) perform tuning on several representative manuscripts (or pooled dev splits) and show results under alternative settings, or (b) report results under at least one alternative hyperparameter set. 3) Lexical filter transparency: report accuracy without lexical filtering, enumerate the number and types of unreachable test targets per text, and present accuracy conditional on reachable targets; consider replacing hard pruning with soft lexicon scoring if pruning drives gains. 4) Auxiliary-task controls: include at least one control auxiliary task (e.g., character-level language modeling or autoencoding on CELEX orthography) and a randomized-label control to test whether gains are phonology-specific. 5) Mechanistic probes: add causal/ablative experiments such as freezing/ablating the shared encoder after MTL training, gating attention during inference, or training attention under MTL with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps; evaluate saliency/attention alignment also on disagreeing outputs. 6) Diagnostics reproducibility: provide seeds and scripts to reproduce parameter-difference heatmaps, saliency matrices, and t-SNE plots; report robustness (multiple seeds/perplexities) and distributional summaries (not just means) for saliency correlations. 7) Evaluation detail: report character-level metrics alongside word-level accuracy, stratify results by word length and manuscript attributes, and clarify data splits and any preprocessing choices. 8) Tone down mechanistic language in the manuscript’s conclusions unless causal probes strengthen the claim—frame results as converging evidence suggestive of attention-like effects rather than proof of equivalence.
transparency_report: Clear / provided: per-text results across 43 manuscripts, model architectures and decoding variants, many hyperparameter values (embedding/LSTM size, dropout, optimizer, batch size, epochs), description of CELEX auxiliary dataset and its size, and mention of public implementation (anonymized link).

Partially provided: t-SNE perplexities are reported for visualizations, and saliency method reference is given (first-derivative); some preprocessing steps (length filtering in training) and lexicon composition (CELEX + training targets) are described with aggregate counts (172 filtered training samples; ~2.25% unreachable targets) but not per-text breakdowns.

Missing / requested for reproducibility: exact random seeds, scripts and parameter settings to reproduce diagnostics (saliency matrices, parameter-difference heatmaps, t-SNE seeds and perplexity grid), full evaluation pipeline and scripts (how per-text splits were created and how metrics computed), explicit repository URL (non-anonymized) with instructions and environment specs (Keras/TensorFlow versions), and code/data to reproduce control analyses (e.g., auxiliary sampling procedure).

Diagnostics reporting: current diagnostic statistics are informative but often reported as means ± std. dev.; distributional properties, per-text diagnostic tables, and analyses on disagreeing-output subsets are not fully reported and should be added.
epistemic_limits: The manuscript's strongest empirical claims about average performance improvements (encoder–decoder > baselines; MTL improves non-attentional variants) rest on extensive per-text experiments and are empirically well supported within the reported setup, but generalization beyond that setup is uncertain. Key epistemic limits are: (1) correlation vs causation: reported parameter/saliency correlations and error overlaps are consistent with MTL inducing focusing-like behavior but do not establish that MTL implements the same computational mechanism as explicit attention—causal interventions are needed to reduce this uncertainty; (2) auxiliary specificity: without controls, it is unclear whether CELEX phonological supervision specifically yields the transfer or whether similar gains would follow from any large auxiliary dataset; (3) sensitivity to experimental choices: hyperparameters tuned on a single dev manuscript, a hard lexical filter that prunes outputs, and a fixed MTL sampling regimen may materially affect outcomes; (4) sample heterogeneity: substantial variance across manuscripts means per-text behavior may diverge from the averages, limiting claims of consistent superiority across dialects/time periods; (5) diagnostic selection bias: saliency and representational visualizations were in places restricted to agreeing outputs or selective examples, limiting inference about the models' behavior on more challenging or discordant cases. These epistemic limits imply that the mechanistic claim should be presented as a hypothesis supported by convergent correlational evidence rather than as a proven equivalence; targeted experiments (statistical robustness, control auxiliaries, causal/ablation probes, and reproducibility artifacts) can narrow these limits.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This empirical paper evaluates character-level encoder–decoder LSTM models for historical spelling normalization on 43 Early New High German texts. It systematically ablates decoding/architecture choices (greedy/beam, lexical filtering, attention, bidirectional encoder) and introduces multi-task learning (MTL) with a grapheme→phoneme auxiliary task (CELEX). Main empirical findings: encoder–decoder variants outperform cited baselines on average; beam + lexical filtering + attention yield cumulative gains in single-task models; MTL improves non-attentional models (often reaching parity with attentive single-task models); adding attention to MTL does not produce additive gains on average. The authors present multiple correlational diagnostics (parameter-difference correlations, error-overlap, high output agreement, saliency correlations, t-SNE) arguing MTL induces attention-like focusing. Results are empirically substantial but heterogeneous across manuscripts and the mechanistic claim remains correlational rather than causal.
strengths: Comprehensive multi-text empirical evaluation: per-text results across 43 manuscripts enable assessment of robustness across diverse small-data regimes.
Systematic architectural ablations: clear decomposition of contributions from greedy vs beam decoding, lexical filtering, attention, and (where used) bidirectional encoding.

Multi-pronged diagnostic analyses: parameter-change correlations, error-overlap accounting, saliency-map correlations, and embedding visualizations provide convergent, interpretable evidence for representational/behavioral similarity between MTL and attention.

Practical relevance: demonstrates that MTL with a large auxiliary dataset (CELEX) can yield average gains on low-resource normalization tasks; implementation details and code release (anonymized) aid reproducibility.
limitations: Causal inference gap: diagnostics are correlational (parameter/saliency correlations, error overlaps, κ agreement) and do not establish that MTL implements the same computational mechanism as explicit attention; no lesion/ablation interventions or causal probes reported to test mechanism.

Auxiliary-task specificity not isolated: only CELEX grapheme→phoneme is used as auxiliary; no control auxiliary tasks (e.g., character LM, autoencoding, randomized-label CELEX) are tested to determine whether gains are phonology-specific or due to generic extra-data regularization.

Hyperparameter/dev-set bias: all hyperparameters were tuned manually on a single manuscript (B) that is then excluded from averages; sensitivity of results to hyperparameter choices and representativeness of B is not demonstrated.

Lexical-filter confound and coverage loss: lexical filtering uses CELEX + training targets and authors report ~2.25% unreachable test targets; impact of hard pruning on reported word-level accuracy is not fully quantified (results with/without filter not fully compared).

Selection and visualization limits: saliency correlations are computed only on subsets where models agree (possible selection bias); t-SNE and saliency methods are sensitive to seeds/hyperparameters and robustness checks are limited.
open_questions: Can the authors provide causal/ablative probes to test the mechanistic claim? Suggested experiments: freeze or ablate shared MTL encoder layers after training, gate or remove the attention module under MTL, or train diagnostic probes to predict attention weights from MTL encoder states.

Are MTL gains specific to CELEX grapheme→phoneme supervision? Please report at least one control auxiliary task (e.g., character-level language modeling, autoencoding, or randomized-label CELEX) and experiments varying auxiliary:main sampling ratios to show phonology-specific transfer versus generic auxiliary-data effects.

How sensitive are the main comparisons to hyperparameter choices? Provide results when hyperparameters are tuned on multiple representative manuscripts or present a small cross-validated hyperparameter sweep to show robustness of Base vs MTL and MTL vs MTL+ATT comparisons.

What is the exact impact of lexical filtering? Provide per-text counts of unreachable targets, accuracy without lexical filtering, and accuracy conditional on reachable targets to quantify any inflation due to output pruning.

Do saliency/attention correlations hold on disagreeing outputs and across random seeds? Please report distributions (not just means ± std) and robustness checks (multiple seeds/perplexities for t-SNE, bootstrap CIs for saliency correlations).

How well do CELEX pronunciations align with the historical orthographic/dialectal variation in the Anselm texts? Provide qualitative or quantitative analysis of CELEX–historical mapping compatibility or stratified MTL effect sizes by apparent orthographic divergence.
consensus_snapshot: Encoder–decoder character-level models outperform cited baselines on average across the 43 manuscripts (Tables 1/4).
MTL using CELEX provides average improvements, with the clearest relative gain for non-attentional models (MTL no-attn frequently matches single-task + attention in aggregates).
Beam search, lexical filtering, and attention give cumulative gains in single-task encoder–decoder models; MTL + attention is not consistently additive in the reported setup.

Multiple correlational diagnostics consistently point toward representational/behavioral resemblance between MTL and attention-enabled models, supporting the hypothesis that MTL induces focusing-like effects.
disagreement_snapshot: Extent of mechanistic claim: reviewers agree evidence is suggestive but differ on whether current diagnostics suffice to assert that MTL 'learns attention'—some view convergent correlations as promising; others require causal probes before stronger wording.

Interpretation of MTL+attention interaction: some reviewers see the average non-additivity as possibly a hyperparameter/tuning artifact, while others consider it meaningful evidence of redundancy or interference—both readings are plausible given present data.

Novelty magnitude: reviewers concur on novelty in combining CELEX G2P MTL with seq2seq normalization across many small texts, but differ on whether this is an incremental empirical contribution or a potentially disruptive mechanistic insight pending stronger causal evidence.
uncertainty_snapshot: Correlational diagnostics vary widely across texts (high std. dev. in reported correlations and overlaps), so averaged correlations may obscure important per-text heterogeneity.
Hyperparameter choices (single-dev tuning) and fixed MTL sampling regimen introduce uncertainty about generalizability across manuscripts and across alternative training conventions.

Output-space pruning via lexical filtering and its reported coverage loss (~2.25%) create uncertainty about how much some accuracy gains rely on constrained decoding versus improved model internalization.
Selection of examples/subsets for diagnostics (e.g., saliency only on agreeing outputs) produces uncertainty about how representative the diagnostics are for challenging or disagreement cases.
source_trace: CELEX auxiliary dataset description and size: Sec. 2 (paper) — CELEX contains ~365,530 wordforms used as grapheme→phoneme supervision.

Empirical performance tables: Table 1 and Table 4 (paper) report mean word-level accuracies and per-text results across 43 manuscripts demonstrating encoder–decoder and MTL numbers referenced in claims C1–C4.

Parameter-difference correlations and saliency analyses: Sec. 5 (paper) and Figures 4–5 — reported statistics (Pearson r, ρ values, κ agreement) and descriptions of saliency methodology referencing Li et al. (2016).

MTL design and sampling regimen: Sec. 3.5 and Sec. 3.6 (paper) — architecture shares encoder/decoder with task-specific classifiers and samples 1 auxiliary instance per main sample; epochs counted by main task.

Relevant prior work and interpretability method: Caruana (1993, 1998) cited for MTL motivation; Li et al. (2016) for first-derivative saliency; Cho et al. / Sutskever et al. for seq2seq foundations — referenced in Secs. 3.5, 5.3, and 3.1 of the paper.
transparency_notes: Paper provides extensive per-text tables, model/decoding variants, and many hyperparameter values (embedding/recurrent sizes, dropout, optimizer settings). Code is said to be released (anonymized link). Missing reproducibility pieces requested by reviewers: exact random seeds, scripts for diagnostics (saliency matrices, parameter-difference heatmaps, t-SNE seeds/perplexities), per-text counts for filtered/truncated training and unreachable test targets, and evaluation scripts to reproduce the reported statistical summaries. Authors should release these artifacts and report robustness checks (multiple seeds, hyperparameter sensitivity) to increase transparency.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Focus editorial scrutiny on whether the manuscript's revisions address core validity threats to the mechanistic claim: (1) paired statistical testing across manuscripts for key comparisons; (2) quantification of lexical-filter coverage loss and presentation of results without hard pruning; (3) sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters (cross-dev tuning or multi-dev sweeps); (4) at least one control auxiliary-task experiment and variation of auxiliary sampling to isolate CELEX-specific effects; (5) causal/ablation probes (shared-layer lesioning or gating attention) to test mechanistic substitution; and (6) reproducibility materials for diagnostics (seeds, scripts). If authors supply these analyses or otherwise temper mechanistic language to match correlational evidence, the paper stands as a valuable empirical contribution. If these issues remain, emphasize scaling back mechanistic claims and foreground empirical benchmarking of MTL+CELEX as an incremental methodological variant.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Prioritize experiments and reporting that materially reduce interpretive uncertainty: 1) Run paired (non-parametric) statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon) across the 43 manuscripts for the main model comparisons and report effect sizes and CIs. 2) Provide results without lexical filtering, per-text counts of unreachable targets, and accuracy conditional on reachable targets; consider soft lexicon scoring alternatives. 3) Demonstrate hyperparameter robustness by tuning on multiple representative manuscripts (or pooled dev splits) and report whether key comparisons hold under alternative settings. 4) Add at least one control auxiliary task (e.g., character LM, autoencoder, or randomized-label CELEX) and vary auxiliary:main sampling ratios to test phonology-specific transfer vs generic effects. 5) Add causal probes: freeze/ablate shared MTL components post-training, gate attention during inference, and compare saliency vs attention on disagreeing outputs. 6) Release reproducibility artifacts for all diagnostics (seeds, scripts, t-SNE parameters) and provide robustness checks (multiple seeds/perplexities, bootstrap CIs). 7) Include complementary metrics (character-error-rate, edit-distance distributions) and stratified analyses (by word length, dialect/time cluster). 8) Tone down mechanistic wording unless causal probes substantiate the claim; present diagnostics as converging, suggestive evidence and outline further work required for mechanistic confirmation.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This manuscript presents a thorough empirical evaluation showing that character-level encoder–decoder models outperform several baselines on 43 Early New High German texts, that beam search + lexical filtering + attention yield cumulative gains in single-task models, and that multi-task learning with CELEX grapheme→phoneme auxiliary data improves non-attentional models—often matching single-task models using attention. The authors provide multiple diagnostics (parameter-change correlations, error overlaps, saliency correlations, t-SNE) suggesting MTL induces attention-like focusing.

Strengths:
- Large-scale per-text benchmark across 43 small, heterogeneous manuscripts enables assessment of robustness and variance. 
- Clear, systematic ablation of decoding and architecture choices with interpretable progression of gains. 
- Multi-faceted diagnostics offering converging evidence beyond accuracy metrics. 
- Practical applicability: MTL+CELEX shows promise for low-resource normalization.

Limitations:
- No causal probes: evidence that MTL 'learns attention' is correlational; lesion/gating experiments are absent. 
- Auxiliary-task specificity untested: only CELEX G2P is used; no control auxiliary tasks to isolate phonology-specific transfer. 
- Hyperparameter tuning performed on a single dev manuscript (B) and applied corpus-wide; sensitivity and representativeness are unverified. 
- Lexical filtering prunes outputs (∼2.25% targets unreachable), potentially inflating word-level accuracy; per-text coverage impacts are not fully reported. 
- Selection bias and visualization sensitivity: saliency correlations computed on agreeing outputs and t-SNE/saliency robustness to seeds/hyperparameters not fully shown.

Open Questions:
1) Please add causal/ablative experiments (e.g., freeze shared encoder, gate attention) to test whether MTL-shared components causally produce the focusing behavior and performance gains. 
2) Provide control auxiliary-task experiments (character LM, autoencoder, or randomized labels) and vary auxiliary:main sampling ratios to determine whether CELEX phonology is specifically responsible for transfer. 
3) Report robustness to hyperparameter choices (tuning on multiple dev texts or pooled dev splits) and whether main comparisons hold under alternative settings. 
4) Quantify lexical-filter effects: per-text unreachable-target counts, accuracy without filter, and conditional accuracies to show whether pruning inflates scores. 
5) Report saliency/attention correlations and diagnostics on disagreeing outputs and across multiple seeds; provide distributional summaries (not only means ± sd). 
6) Provide analysis of CELEX–historical alignment (qualitative examples or stratified effect sizes) to assess compatibility with Early New High German orthographic/dialectal variation.

Transparency:
The paper provides detailed per-text tables, architectural descriptions, and many hyperparameters. Code release is signaled (anonymized). Missing reproducibility artifacts include exact random seeds, scripts for computing diagnostics (saliency, parameter differences, t-SNE), per-text counts for filtered/truncated samples, and evaluation scripts used to produce aggregate statistics. Authors should add these and robustness checks (multiple seeds/hyperparameters) for diagnostics.

(End of meta-review.)

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. As with the above reviewer issues, it’s a case-by-case evaluation: some things in the list below may be appropriate in a given context, given that they are sufficiently motivated. We provide codes for different types of issues (e.g. M1, G2…) that can be referenced in discussions.
